about: THE CREW'S WORDS (Design/content/BRIEF.md, BRIEF_2.md), written 4 Oct 2026: a draft for the user to overwrite. Every title, intention, line and option label of Data/encounters/crew_793.json has its entry here under the card's id; 'art.<card id>' says in one line what the picture on the card shows; '<label key>.out' is what comes of an option, as a plain fact ('.fail' when a chance goes against the merchant): the engine shows only the effects' own facts today, so the .out lines wait for an outcome key (the report's needs). The five voices: the steersman, a baptised Frisian, says the worst first and then what can be done; the Dane says less than he means and gives no answers; the mate, a Saxon, has few words and one proverb; the lookout, a young Englishman schooled by monks, is homesick for books; the hand is an ordinary man. Words inside single quotation marks are quoted from the texts of texts_793.json or from a translation out of copyright, named in the card's note; the rest is ours. entries.text: The reckoning
The cargo is sold. The mate speaks for the men: they want what the tally says they are owed.
Evening at a mooring: the mate stands in the boat holding out a notched tally stick; three men sit on the thwarts behind him, not looking at the merchant; a small iron-bound chest on the stern board.
Thirty pennies are cut on the tally stick by the mast, a penny a man for every four days.
The cargo is sold and the silver is in the chest, where the men can hear it. They ask for their share now, before the alehouse asks for it.
They know about the Wōkerer. They say he has a full plate, and they have an oar each.
Count it out on the thwart (30 d)
Half now, the rest at the next landing (15 d)
Open a cask of the cargo's ale tonight; silver at the next sale
Ask them to wait
Thirty pennies go round in fours and fives. The mate cuts the tally stick across and throws the old half over the side. Nobody says thank you. It was owed.
Fifteen pennies. The mate splits the tally down its length and gives you one half, with the notches still owed. He keeps the other.
The cask is empty by the time the fires ashore go out. In the morning the tally stick has the same notches on it, and everyone aboard can count.
The mate nods and goes forward. You do not hear what he says to them. You hear what they do not say back.
The promise
You promised the men their pay at the next landing. This is the next landing.
A quay in the morning: the mate holds up his half of a split tally stick beside the merchant's half; the notches match.
You said the next landing. This is a landing.
I can see the chest as well as you can. Tell me what I am to tell them.
Pay what was promised (20 d)
Cut a bolt of the cargo's cloth among them: worth more than they are owed
Tell them there is nothing yet
The two halves of the tally are laid together, the pennies counted along the notches, and both halves burnt on the fire-stone. A word kept is remembered longer than a wage.
A bolt of Frisian cloth makes four cloaks' lengths and a quarrel about the selvedge. On their own coast rents are paid in cloaks. Nobody calls it short.
They stay. They row as men row who are counting something. The mate says he will ask once more, and that he has never yet had to ask three times.
In the morning one thwart is empty and one bundle gone. He took nothing that was not his. He left the oar shipped and dry, which was a kind of message.
A wage or a share
The house is doing well. The mate asks whether the men might have a part of the venture instead of a wage.
The boat moored and well laden in afternoon light; the mate and the steersman sit on the quay edge facing the merchant, the mate holding up one finger of his ten.
The men would sooner have a part of the venture than a penny for every four days. A man with a share watches the cargo in the rain.
And a man with a share argues about where to sell it. I say that against myself.
Men who put their goods in one keel and divide the gain have a name for it in the north. A man there is known by whom he owned a ship with.
A tenth of each season's gain, shared among them at Martinmas
Keep the wage, but each man may carry a bundle of his own to trade
A wage is a wage
It is agreed with a handclasp over the mast-step, the steersman as witness. By evening every man aboard has an opinion about the price of wine at Lundenwic.
Four bundles appear under the thwarts within a week: combs, a cheese, a length of cloth, something Ravn will not show. They take up no more room than the men's hopes.
The mate says a wage is at least a thing a man can count. He does not say it as if he were pleased.
Martinmas
The sailing season is over. The men are paid for it now, or they are owed.
A grey November strand: boats being hauled up on rollers, smoke from a slaughter yard behind; the merchant counts coins into the mate's open hand beside the hauled-out boat.
Martinmas. The boats come up the strand, the cattle go under the knife, and every master on this coast is counting out silver or reasons.
Four men, one season. You have the tally.
And the tenth part you promised. The men have been working the sum since Michaelmas, each to a different answer.
Pay the season out, and something over for each man (40 d)
Pay what the tally says and no more (24 d)
Ask them to carry it on the tally till Easter

Forty pennies. The something over buys a goose, and the goose is eaten with the hull for a table. Three of the four say they will be at the boat when the geese go north. The fourth says he will think about it, which from him is the same.
Twenty-four pennies, counted twice. The tally stick goes on the fire. Each man has what he was promised and no reason to say more.
A winter is a long time to carry a notch. The mate says he will tell them, and that he would rather have told them anything else.
The Wōkerer's day and the men's
The Wōkerer's day is near and the men's day is past. There is silver enough for one of them.
The purse emptied on a thwart in two unequal piles; the mate points forward at the men, the steersman points over his shoulder at a hall on the river bank.
The Wōkerer's day is close and the men's day is past. There is silver for one of them. I would sooner he went short. He has never rowed you off a lee shore.
The worst first. The count can take the boat. The men can only take themselves. Lose the boat and nobody is ever paid again.
The men first (24 d)
The count first; the men at the next sale
Half to the men now, and keep the rest for the count (12 d)
The men are paid. The mate says it was rightly done. The steersman says nothing and looks up the river toward the count's hall, as a man looks at weather.
The silver stays in the chest for the count. The mate tells the men. One of them says the count has never bailed, and nobody laughs.
Twelve pennies to the men and a half-tally to each side. Nobody is content and nobody is wronged, which the steersman says is the usual shape of a fair thing.
A man looks landward
The hand has had word from home. He asks to be there before the autumn storms.
A summer sea with the low line of a marsh coast far off; a young oarsman rests on his oar and looks at the land instead of at the stroke.
A man off a Frisian boat told me at the last landing. My father cannot walk since the spring, and the hay stands. I am the only son who is not under the turf.
I do not ask to be paid off. I ask to be home before the autumn storms, and back at your oar by Easter.
A man is master at home. A pair of goats and a patched roof, the old words say, and they say it better than I do.
Give your word: home by Michaelmas
Send silver to his father by the next Frisian boat instead (8 d)
The season is short and so is the crew. After Martinmas
He takes your hand on it and rows the rest of the watch as if the boat were lighter. Ravn says his verse through, to no one: better a house, though a hut it be.
Eight pennies will hire a neighbour's sons for the hay. He thanks you properly. He still looks at the land when he thinks you are looking at the sail.
He says he understands, in the voice men use for that. For some days he is the first at his oar and the last to speak.
Michaelmas
The hand reminds you of your word. A boat for his own coast lies in the harbour.
An autumn quay with two boats: the hand stands between them with his bundle already tied, cap in hand, facing the merchant; yellow leaves on the water.
Michaelmas, or near enough that the saint will not quarrel. You gave me your word in the summer.
A boat for the terp country lies three berths down. Her master will take a man who can row.
We sail a man short if he goes. I would let him go. A man kept against a promise rows like a sack.
Pay him what is on his tally and put him on the other boat (10 d)
Offer him half as much again to stay till Martinmas (6 d)
Tell him the word was given in a better month
Ten pennies and his own knife, sharpened. He steps across to the other boat without looking back, because he means to come back. The men watch you do it.
He weighs six pennies against his father's hay and takes the pennies. He is not proud of it, and for a while he lets you see that.
He hears you out, shakes his head and picks up his bundle. A promise was made, he says, and he would rather keep his end of it than be paid for yours.
He does not argue. He goes back to his thwart and sits with his hands between his knees. The mate finds something to do at the far end of the boat.
He does not argue. In the morning his thwart is empty and the boat for the terp country has sailed. The men heard him go, and none of them woke you.
A man on the mooring post
The hand you sent home in the autumn is back, and asks for his oar.
A spring morning at the mooring: a man sits on the post with a bundle and a round cheese on his knees; behind him the boat with fresh black tar on her strakes.
A man is sitting on the mooring post with a bundle and a cheese the size of a helmet.
The hay was got in, the old man is up on two sticks, and my mother says a son who eats this much should do it at sea. Is my oar taken?
I see you found another back for my thwart. I can row behind him.
His oar is his
Take him back, and buy his mother's cheeses for the hold (4 d)
The oar is taken
He steps aboard as if he had gone ashore for water. The cheese is cut that evening and judged, by Ravn, to be the first good thing out of Frisia since the cloak.
Three more wheels come down from the terp on his brother's back. His mother has never sold a cheese farther than the next mound, and now they are bound for Lundenwic.
He looks at the boat a while, nods, and carries his cheese to the next mooring. A man who can row finds an oar by evening. It will not be yours.
When the vessel stands
Home. The men can see their own roofs from the boat, and the cargo is still aboard.
Dorestat's dam heads at dusk: the boat just made fast, women and children coming down the planking with a lamp; the English lookout alone on the bow, watching other men's families.
In my country they teach boys a saying about your people. 'Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife, when the vessel stands; his ship is come, and her husband to home.'
'She calls him in, washes his weedy garment, and to him gives new raiment.' It stands in a list of things that are always so, near frost and fire.
It is true as far as the washing. Nobody in England has asked her what she says about the smell.
Let them go home tonight; the cargo keeps till morning
Two ashore and two aboard, turn about
Unload first
The boat lies alone at the dam head with her cargo under the sail. In the morning the men are back before the toll man, washed, in dry clothes, and slow.
Two go up the planking and two stay with the cargo and listen to the town. At midnight they change. Nobody sleeps much and nothing is stolen.
It is dark before the last bale is up. The steersman says a hold emptied is a hold nobody can rob. His wife, at the dam head, says something shorter.
Pork in Lent
A fast day for three of them and not for the fourth: Ravn has meat on the fire and the steersman will not sit downwind of it.

The boat at rest on a grey March day, a small fire on the flat fire-stone amidships; the Dane turns a piece of pork on his knife, the steersman stands upwind with folded arms, the mate looks at neither.
He has pork on the fire-stone in Lent. Either he eats it downwind or I do not eat at all, and I am the one who steers.
My belly keeps no priest's calendar, and the pig's dead already. It won't be less dead at Easter.

In Saxony the king's law is short: 'If any one, out of contempt for Christianity, shall have despised the holy Lenten fast and shall have eaten flesh, let him be punished by death.' The mate has stopped chewing.
I eat what the steersman eats, where a priest can see. Ask me nothing else.
Order the meat put away till Easter
Buy the pork off him for the stores: in salt it will keep till Easter (2 d)
Each man keeps his own custom: he eats in the bow
Ravn wraps the meat and eats bread with the rest. He chews it as a man chews a debt.
Two pennies, and the pork goes into the brine tub. Ravn says it is the first time anyone has paid him not to eat. The steersman blesses the fish with some feeling.
He eats in the bow, with the wind taking the smell forward. The steersman says he could steer by it, and for the rest of the day he does.
A horn of ale and a prayer
The land is dropping astern. Ravn wants to pour ale over the stem for his god; the steersman wants a prayer to Saint Martin.
Open water in a fresh morning wind, the coast a thin line astern; the Dane at the stem with a drinking horn tilted over the water, the steersman at the steering oar with his cap in his free hand.
The land is a line astern. Ravn has a horn of ale in his fist and is looking at the stem, not at his mouth.
Ashore I'll try any god you like. On open water I ask the one with the hammer. He has heard my voice before.
Saint Martin has this boat. I named her to him at Traiectum and I paid for the candle.
Let him pour
The steersman says the prayer; every man uncovers his head
The sea is wide enough for a prayer and a horn of ale
The ale goes over the stem and the sea takes it without comment. The steersman crosses himself three times, once for each man who watched and said nothing.
The steersman says the words and the others uncover their heads. Ravn uncovers his too, drinks the ale himself, and says that somebody may as well have it.
A prayer from the stern and a horn of ale from the bow. The boat goes on between them. Each man is sure the other's part did no harm and his own did some good.
One foot in the water
Ravn tells the steersman a story about the steersman's own king. Both of them look at you.
Evening at sea, two men on one thwart: the Dane telling a story with one bare foot held over the bilge water as if over a font; the steersman staring straight ahead.

Your own king had one foot in the priest's water, and then he asked where his fathers were. In hell, said the priest. So he took the foot out again, and said he'd sooner sit with them than with a few beggars in heaven.
Radbod. Yes. And he is where he chose to be, and my grandfather with him. I think about that more than you do.
The monks tell it as a warning. Told by a Northman across a rowing bench it sounds like something else.
Laugh with Ravn
Say that a king who goes to hell for the company is still in hell
Ask each of them what his own father would have said
Ravn is pleased, and it shows. The steersman takes the next watch himself and the one after, and speaks to nobody about the course.
The steersman nods once. Ravn says that company is most of what a man gets anywhere, and lets it drop.

Ravn's father would have asked what the priest was selling. The steersman's father was baptised at sixty and said it was like being told he had spelled his own name wrong all his life. They are still talking when the watch changes.
How a Saxon is made a Christian
Somebody has asked the mate how he was baptised. He answers, which he does not often do.
Dusk on the water: the big Saxon mate stands to speak with one hand lifted, as if answering a question from a bank; in the cloud behind him, men waist-deep in a river and spearmen on the shore.
They stand you in the river in your shirt, with the king's spearmen on the bank. The priest asks, and you answer. Then you are a Christian and may go home, if there is one.
'Ec forsacho allum dioboles uuercum and uuordum, Thunaer ende Uoden ende Saxnote.' I forsake them. Those were the words.
He named them out loud to give them up? That's not how I'd stop a god listening.
Ask him to say all of it, slowly
Ask him whether he meant it
Leave it there

He says it through, question and answer, in the flat voice of a man walking a boundary. The lookout moves his lips after him. It is the first time it has been said on this boat with nobody holding a spear.
He looks at the water for a long time. 'I meant the part about going home,' he says, and goes forward to see to the anchor, which does not need seeing to.
The talk turns to the price of rope. The mate looks at you once, as a man does who has been spared something.
Thunder
Thunder along the coast. Ravn is glad of it and the steersman is praying with his teeth shut. Both are holding on.
A squall at sea in late afternoon: rain driving sideways, one fork of lightning over a dark shore; the Dane hauls a sheet and grins upward, the steersman is braced at the oar with his eyes shut.
Thunder walks along the coast and the rain comes in sideways. Ravn is grinning into it. The steersman has let go of nothing and is praying with his teeth shut.
He's driving tonight! Listen to the wheels.
It is weather. God sends it, the saints turn it, and you will hold that sheet or I will find a baptised man who can.
Let each call on his own, as long as the sheet is held
Silence on the thwarts; the steersman gives the words
Say that even the bishop calls the fifth day by the thunderer's name
One of them shouts at the sky and the other mutters at it. The sheet is held, the squall goes through, and both of them are sure who turned it.
The steersman calls the strokes and the saints by turns, in one voice. Ravn holds the sheet with his mouth shut and his face turned up.
The steersman starts to answer and stops, counting the days of the week on his fingers. Ravn laughs so hard he nearly loses the sheet.
The white shirt
The steersman asks Ravn, not for the first time, whether he will ever be baptised. Ravn says he has been.

The Dane on a thwart holding up three fingers, daylight; in the cloud behind him a row of Northmen in white shirts before a king's high seat, the last of them holding a shirt of sacking at arm's length.
The priest at the last landing asked me whether your soul was in any hands yet.
I've been baptised. Three times! At the king's Easter court they give a Northman a white shirt, new, and a gift, and a lord to stand beside him.
The third year there were more of us than shirts, and I got a thing sewn out of a sack, and I told them I'd been washed there before and always dressed like a man, and that this was a swineherd's.
The steersman opens his mouth and shuts it again.
Ask what became of the first two shirts
Tell him not to tell that one where a priest can hear
Ask what a white shirt of that linen fetches in the north
He sold the first at Dorestat to a man who wanted to be buried in it. The second he wore until it was more hole than shirt. He says both washings took equally well.
Ravn says priests have heard it. It was a priest who told the king, and the king who laughed. The steersman does not think that makes it better.
Six pennies in the north, he says, if it has never been worn in a river. Eight if the buyer has not heard where it came from.
Short of the font
The priest of the landing says there is a way for your heathen to deal with Christians without being baptised.
A wooden church door at a landing in daylight: the priest on the step with his thumb raised to make a cross; the Dane below him, bareheaded, considering; the steersman a pace behind.

Your Northman may not eat at a Christian table here, and half the town will not deal with a boat that carries him. There is a way short of the font. I sign him with the cross, and he may stand in the church door and hear. The washing can wait until he asks for it.
They do this at Sliaswic. A man's marked, he trades with both kinds, and he's washed when he's dying and can do no more harm to either god.
It is half a thing. I would rather half than none.
Let the priest sign him, since Ravn is willing
Give the priest something for his poor and leave Ravn as he is (4 d)
He is a good hand as he is

The priest's thumb goes across Ravn's forehead, breast and shoulders. Ravn stands it as a horse stands shoeing. That evening he eats at the host's table, and the host's wife serves him first to see what will happen. Nothing does.
Four pennies for the poor at the church door. The priest takes them and says God can wait longer than a merchant can. Ravn, outside, asks what it cost, and nods.
The priest says he will pray for all four of you, with a weight on the number. Ravn says nothing until the boat is cast off, and then only that it was well done.
A cough in the night
The hand has coughed through two watches. The mate does not like the sound of it.
Night at sea under a half moon: the hand hunched at his oar with a fist to his mouth, the mate turned round on the next thwart to look at him; the men's breath smoking in the cold.
The hand has coughed through two watches. He says it is the salt. It does not sound like salt.
I have heard that cough in a camp. In three days half the tents had it. Get him dry, or get him ashore.
Give him the dry place under the foredeck and the spare cloak
Warm a cup of the cargo's ale or mead for him over the fire-stone
Tell him to row it off
He sleeps under the foredeck with two cloaks over him and coughs less toward morning. The spare cloak comes back smelling of him, and nobody minds.
A cup is warmed on the fire-stone and he drinks it holding it in both hands. The others watch the cup go by. By dawn the cough has loosened.
He rows. He coughs on the pull and breathes on the return, and the stroke goes ragged behind him. The mate looks at you once, and then at the sky.
Fever aboard
The hand burns and shakes and cannot row. What is done with him today decides whether he lives.
Grey daylight at sea: the hand lies in the stern under a fold of sail, his face wet and red; the mate kneels over him with a wet rag; one oar is shipped and idle.
He burns and shakes and does not know the boat. He rows for no one today.
A leech would bleed him and a priest would pray. We have a knife and an Our Father. I would sooner he had rest and a fire.
Rest him in the stern under the spare sail
Put in to the nearest shore and lie a day by a fire
Keep him at his oar: the work will sweat it out
Two days under the spare sail. On the third morning he asks what there is to eat, is told, and complains about it. The mate says that is how you know.
He is quiet in the night and the men take it for sleep. At first light the mate folds the sail back, looks, and folds it over again.
A day lost on a shingle beach, with a driftwood fire and the boat drawn up. He sweats it out between two cloaks. By evening he is cursing the smoke, which the steersman calls a good sign.
The fire is lit and he is laid beside it, and he dies there in the afternoon with dry land under him. It was the right thing to do. It did not help.
He rows the fever out of himself by evening, grey as tallow, and sleeps where he sits. He lives. He does not forget who kept him on the thwart.
He rows until the oar stops. The man behind him takes it out of his hands. Nobody aboard says anything to you for the rest of that day.
The leech and the knots
The men are in poor health. A leech at the landing offers his craft; there is also a woman up the lane.

A landing in thin daylight: a leech sits on an upturned tub with a small knife, a bowl and a bundle of dried herbs laid out on a cloth; behind him, up a lane, an old woman in a doorway with knotted cords hanging from the lintel.
Two of the men have sores that will not close, and all four are slow. At the landing a leech has laid out his knife and his bowl. Up the lane a woman ties knots over the sick for a penny.
Bad blood and wet feet. I let a little from the arm, give wormwood in ale, and they keep off salt meat for a week. Three pennies for the boat.
The leech I can stand. The woman's knots are on the bishop's list of forbidden things, and I will not lie under them.
Pay the leech (3 d)
Send to the woman with the knots (1 d)
Broth, a dry floor and two days' sleep
He bleeds each man a cupful and doses them with something bitter in ale. In three days the sores are closing and the men are quarrelling again, which is health.
He bleeds each man a cupful. They are paler for it and no better, and the leech says the moon was wrong. He keeps the three pennies.
She ties a knotted cord round each man's wrist and says words nobody asks her to repeat. The men feel better at once. The steersman sleeps in the boat.
Broth with barley in it, a dry floor, and nothing to pull. It costs two days. The men come back to the boat walking like men who have been asked for nothing.
The body
The hand is dead and lies under the spare sail. He was baptised. The nearest church is days away.
Morning at sea in flat light: a long shape sewn in a cloak lies along the bottom boards; the steersman stands over it with his cap off, the Dane sits apart looking at the water; no land in sight.
He lies along the bottom boards under the spare sail. The boat is seven paces long, and there is nowhere aboard her that is not beside him.
He was baptised. He should lie in church ground with a priest over him. That is days off, and the dead do not keep. Now I have said both.
The sea took a king once, in a ship, with gold at his knees. It has taken worse men than this one. But he was yours, not mine.
The king's law for the conquered Saxons says that the bodies of Christians are to be carried to the church's ground and not to the mounds of the heathen. It does not say what a boat is to do.
Keep him aboard and make for the nearest church
Give him to the sea: sewn in his cloak, a stone at his feet, the steersman to say the Our Father
Land on the nearest shore and lay him under stones above the tide mark
He stays aboard, sewn in his cloak, with his head to the stem. The men row as hard as they have ever rowed, and nobody sits on that side.

Sewn in his cloak, with a ballast stone at his feet. The steersman says the Our Father and stumbles once. The cloak goes down pale, then green, then is not there. The mate cuts the dead man's notches from the tally and keeps the piece.

A strand nobody knows the name of. Stones are carried up above the weed line until the heap is the length of a man, and the steersman cuts a cross on a driftwood stake. The lookout learns the place by a headland and a split rock, in case anyone ever asks.
Church ground
You have brought the dead hand to a landing. He must be put in the ground today.

A small wooden church on a low mound under a grey sky: an open grave by the fence, a priest in the doorway with his arms folded, the steersman with one hand raised to swear; the wrapped body on a litter of two oars held by the other men.
I do not know him. Who says he was baptised, and where? I have put a stranger in this ground before on a shipmaster's word, and had to answer for it.
There is no church here and no priest. The Christian traders of the place keep a strip of ground of their own behind the boat-sheds, and bury one another.
I saw the cross on him every day he rowed. I will swear to it on whatever they hold holy here.
Pay for the grave, a mass and bread for the poor in his name (6 d)
The steersman swears to his baptism, and the crew dig the grave themselves
Leave two pennies with the gravedigger and catch the tide (2 d)

A grave inside the fence, a mass with his name in it, and bread given at the door to whoever comes. The men stand through all of it. Afterwards the mate says it was done right, and he does not say much.

The steersman swears to it before those who keep the ground, and the men dig, turn about, with a borrowed spade and the boat's own bailer. It is not as deep as a gravedigger would have it. It is deep enough.
Two pennies in the gravedigger's hand, and the tide will not wait. From the water you can see him still leaning on his spade, not digging. The steersman watches until the land hides it.
The dead man's share
The mother of the hand who died has found the boat. His share and his things are still aboard.

A quay in a Frisian port in the afternoon: a small old woman in a dark headcloth stands at the boat's side with both hands on the gunwale; the mate holds out a folded cloak with a knife and a comb laid on top of it.
They told me at the last boat in. I did not come to shout. I came for what he earned and what he owned, and to hear where you put him.
Sixty days on his tally. Fifteen pennies, a knife, a cloak and a comb. I have kept them apart since the day.
Pay his whole share, give her his things and tell her where he lies (15 d)
Pay the share less what his burying cost (9 d)
Give her the knife, the cloak and the comb, and promise the silver
Fifteen pennies counted into her apron; the knife, the cloak, the comb. You tell her where he lies and how it was done. She asks whether he was any good at it, the rowing. The mate says he was.
Nine pennies and his things. She counts the coins, looks at you, and counts them again. She does not ask what the six were for. She has buried people; she knows what it costs and who pays.
She takes the cloak and smells it, and puts the knife and the comb inside it. A promise, she says, is what her husband left her too. She will be on this quay whenever your boat is.
What Ravn wants done
Some days after the burial Ravn tells you what he wants if he dies aboard.
A calm sea at dusk: the Dane at his oar speaking without turning his head, the merchant beside him listening; far astern a thin thread of smoke rising from some shore.
If I die in this boat, no priest, no water on my head, no hole inside a fence. Fire, if there is a shore for it. If not, the sea, and my knife with me.
In the king's Saxon lands a man who burns a body after the heathen custom pays for it with his life. What a Frisian count would do about smoke on his own strand, nobody aboard knows.
Give him your word
No fire where the count's men can see smoke: the sea you can promise
Tell him to stay alive
He nods and goes on rowing. Nothing more is said about it, then or later. He rows next to you for the rest of that watch, which he has not done before.
He thinks about it for forty strokes. The sea is not a bad hall, he says, and nobody there asks what a man believed. He holds out his hand and you take it.
He almost laughs. That is the plan, he says. But he looks at the steersman's cross for a while afterwards, and then at you.
Green bread
The stores are nearly gone and land is days off. The mate asks how the rest is to be shared.
Open sea at noon: the mate holds up a nearly empty bread sack by its corners; on the thwart, a heel of loaf furred green beside a knife; four men looking at it, no land on the horizon.
Bread for two days if nobody is hungry, and what there is has a green coat. The men will take short commons from a master who takes them too. Not otherwise.
Cattle know when to leave the grass, the old words say, and a man's belly never learned it. Mine's no wiser than the next.
Half a ration each till landfall, yours with theirs
Lines over the side and the small net
Open a cheese from the cargo

Half a heel of loaf each at noon, yours cut last and no larger. Ravn says his verse over his share: 'The herds know well when home they shall fare, and then from the grass they go; but the foolish man his belly's measure shall never know aright.' Then he eats slowly, to show that he heard himself.
Mackerel, on bare hooks with a shred of red cloth, faster than they can be hauled. They are split and eaten half raw off the fire-stone. For one evening the boat smells of something better than men.
Four lines over the side from noon to dusk, and one small whiting between them. The steersman says the fish have heard about the bread.
One of the cargo's cheeses is cut in four on the thwart. It was meant for a richer table. It does more good here, and every man aboard knows what it cost you.
A farm above the strand
The men are hungry and the boat lies off a lone farm. The farmer is watching, and has sent a child running inland.

The boat at anchor off a shingle strand in afternoon light; above it a single turf-roofed farm, the farmer standing in his yard with an axe held low, a child running away up a path; the lookout in the bow lifting a horn to his mouth.
A turf roof, a byre, smoke. A man in the yard with an axe held low, not raised. A child is running inland, which means there are neighbours.
By the West Saxons' law a stranger who leaves the road and neither shouts nor blows a horn is taken for a thief, to be killed or ransomed. I would blow the horn. I would blow it twice.
Blow the horn and walk up with silver in an open hand (6 d)
Blow the horn and offer a bundle of whetstones for bread and a sheep
Blow the horn and ask plainly for what he can spare
The horn, then open hands, then silver. He bites a penny, calls the child back, and sells you bread, a crock of butter and half a smoked ewe. His wife asks for news. She has had none since the hay.

He turns the whetstones over as if they were loaves. Stone like that does not come to his strand twice in a lifetime. Bread, and a sheep on the hoof, and he carries the sheep down to the boat himself.

He hears you out with the axe still in his hand, and then puts it down. Yesterday's bread and a bowl of curds, handed over the wall. He will not take thanks. He says he has been hungry in a boat himself.
He hears you out, and says he has four mouths and a bad year, and that the boat looks better fed than his byre. The neighbours are coming over the hill. You go back to the boat.
Wheat in a hungry port
There is famine ashore and wheat in the hold. The men are watching what you do with it.

A river port in thin spring light: gaunt people sitting along the quay's edge, a church door behind them; in the boat, full sacks under the sail, the mate standing with one hand on a sack and his eyes on the merchant.
People are sitting along the quay who have no reason to be there, except that boats come to it. Children with old faces. The sacks in the hold are tight and smell of summer.
I have seen an army eat a district bare, and what the district looked like the spring after. It looked like this quay. The men are watching what you do with the sacks. So am I.
Grain is as dear as anyone can remember, and no law says what it may fetch. So it lies between you and the Judge, which is a harder market.
The king has set it: four pennies the measure of wheat and no more, and his own grain cheaper. A count who wants to seem diligent could ask what was charged on this quay.
Give a sack at the church door, through the priest
Tell the men it goes at the king's price and no more
It goes to whoever pays most: that is what a market is
A sack is carried up to the church door and the priest shares it out by the bowl. Your name is not said, as you asked, and is known to everyone by evening. The mate carries the sack himself.
The men nod. The king's price is a price a man can say aloud at home. The steersman says he will stand by the measure himself and see it struck level.
Nobody argues; it is your wheat. The mate goes ashore without asking and comes back late. In the morning his own bread for the day is gone from his bundle, and he rows on water.
Frost on the thwarts
A night watch in the cold months. The men are stiff, wet and a long way from a fire.
A winter night at sea under hard stars: white rime on the thwarts and the oar looms, four men hunched in short cloaks with their breath in clouds; a black coast with no light on it.
The thwarts are white. The oars burn the hands, and then the hands stop feeling them. Nobody has spoken since the stars came out.
The king himself asked what use these Frisian cloaks were: too short to cover a man in bed, no good against the wind on a horse, and sold at the long cloak's price. He should try one in a boat.
Fire is what a man needs who comes in with frozen knees. That's an old one. Nobody ever made one about rowing harder.
Put in to the shore and light a fire till the sky greys
Break out a bolt of the cargo's cloth for wraps: the salt may spoil it
Two at the oars, turn about, till they are warm

A beach, driftwood, a fire fit to roast an ox. The men turn themselves like loaves. Ravn says his verse to the flames: 'Fire he needs who with frozen knees has come from the cold without.' At first grey they shove off, dry on one side.
A bolt is opened and wound round four men like swaddling. It keeps the wind off. At dawn it is rolled again, damp at the edge and no worse, and it will sell.

A bolt is opened and wound round four men. It keeps the wind off, and by dawn the spray has gone through every fold. Cloth stiff with salt sells to nobody. The men keep it for cloaks, and are warm until spring.
Two pull while two beat their arms, and they change at every hundred strokes. It keeps the blood moving and nobody sleeps. By dawn they are warm, emptied, and not grateful.
Ice at the piles
The harbour is freezing. Ice that closes on a hull can open her seams.

A harbour at dawn in hard frost: grey skin ice between the mooring piles with the boat held in it; the steersman kneels on the quay pressing the ice with an oar blade; behind him, men with log rollers waiting to be hired.
There is skin ice between the piles this morning, and it did not go at noon. Ice that closes on a boat finds her seams and opens them like a knife in an oyster.
She will be nipped. Not tonight, maybe; the night after. Out on rollers is five pennies. A sprung plank is twelve and a week. I have said the dear one too, so you can choose.
Praise ice when you've crossed it, they say. Not before, and not from inside a boat.
Hire the strand's men and their rollers and haul her out (5 d)
The crew break the ice round her every dawn
Leave her: it will thaw
Eight men, six rollers and a great deal of shouting, and she sits on the strand with her keel dry. By the next morning the ice has closed over the place where she lay.
Every dawn the men go round her with poles and the anchor stone, breaking it back. Wet to the knee in frost, daily. She takes no harm. They do.
It freezes, groans for two nights, and thaws on the third day with a south wind. She floats free with her seams tight. The steersman says nothing, at some length.
The ice closes on her in the night with a sound like a door. When it thaws a strake is sprung at the bow and she weeps at every nail. The wright wants twelve pennies and does not hurry.
A true song
A cold evening at sea. The lookout knows an English song made by a man who had sat where he sits.
Dusk at sea in winter: the lookout at the prow with his hood up and ice on the stem beside him, his mouth open in speech; grey rollers, and one white swan far off on the water.
There is a song in my country that a man made about this. He begins: 'I can sing of myself a true song, of my voyages telling.' True is the word he puts first.
'Benumbed by the cold, oft the comfortless night-watch hath held me at the prow of my craft.' I used to think he said too much. I had not kept a night watch then.
Hear it through
Say it in summer, when a man can laugh at it
He says it through, slower than he speaks, and the men stop beating their arms to listen. When he comes to the man on land who knows nothing of all this, the mate grunts as if he had been named.
He shuts his mouth and pulls his hood down. A cold song for a warm day, he says after a while: that is not how songs work. But he keeps it.
No wind
Becalmed since dawn. The men have nothing to do and have begun on each other.
A glassy sea at midday with the sail hanging in folds: two men splashing in the water alongside, one of them holding the gunwale; the mate with his arms folded; a pair of bone dice on a thwart.
The sail hangs like washing. The sea is so flat that the boat's own reflection is tiresome. Somebody has said something about somebody's snoring, and it was not taken well.
Idle men are worse than tired ones. Give them a thing to win or a thing to pull. I do not much mind which.
The man in my song swam against his friend Breca for a boast, nights together in the open sea, in his mail, with a sword in his hand. I only say what the song says.
A swimming match round the boat, a cup of ale to the winner
Out oars: an hour's pull earns the evening ale
Let them dice for their knives
Three times round the boat. The steersman wins by a length, and the hand says he was held by the foot, which is true. The ale is shared four ways anyway, and everyone is clean, which helps.

The lookout swims like a man schooled by monks. The steersman hauls him in by the hair, and remarks that the law prices a grip on a man's hair at two shillings and says nothing of when it is the only handle. He coughs water until evening.
An hour at the oars across water like a floor. The boat moves, which is something. The mate counts the stroke and is seen, briefly, to be content.
The knives change hands twice and end where they began. It takes most of the afternoon, and a great deal of argument about what a bone die may be said to have shown.
The hand loses his knife on a throw he says rolled off the thwart. The lookout says the bilge is part of the board. By the ninth hour they have stopped speaking to each other.
A board on the thwart
Ravn has cut a board of squares into a thwart and shaken out a bag of bone pegs. He is looking for someone to play.

A quiet afternoon at sea: a grid of squares scratched into a thwart, bone pegs set out on it with one taller piece in the middle; the Dane sits astride the thwart on one side of the board, and the other side is empty.
A board of squares cut into the thwart with a knife point. One bone king in the middle with his men round him, and twice as many set against him at the edges.
The king must get out to the edge and the others must shut him in. One side's easier, and I'll not say which. Sit, sit!
Sit down opposite him
Let him teach the lookout, and watch the moves
Play if you like, but no silver on the board in this boat
You take the attackers and shut his king in after a long afternoon. He looks at the board for some time, then sets the pegs again and says: once more. From him that is praise.
His king walks out through a gap you did not know you had left. He shows you where it was, without being asked, and sets the pegs again. He has enjoyed himself.
The lookout loses five games and wins the sixth, and cannot be spoken to for pride. You have watched the moves. Ravn now has two men aboard to beat instead of none.
He shrugs and plays for nothing, which he says is how kings play. The pegs click all afternoon. Nobody loses a penny or his temper.
Three wonders
At anchor in the evening the men are telling wonders for a cup of ale. You are the judge.

The boat at anchor in a creek at dusk with a small fire on the fire-stone: three men leaning in, their faces lit, the Dane holding his hands wide apart to show the size of something; a single cup on the thwart between them.

Where the Rhine breaks into the sea there is an island, and on it they keep the bones of a king out of the north who came raiding in my forefathers' day. A man so big no horse could carry him. They show the bones to travellers. I have seen a thigh.
Men landed on an island with no name, grey, bare, a little sand, and they made fast and lit a fire and sat down to eat. The island felt the fire and went under. It was a fish!

A sparrow flies in at one door of the king's hall in winter, through the warmth and the firelight, and out at the other into the storm. A king's counsellor in my country said that is a man's life: what went before and what follows, we do not know.
The cup to the king's bones
The cup to the island that was a fish
The cup to the sparrow

The cup goes to the steersman, who drinks it as if it were owed. Ravn asks whether the thigh is sold by weight. The steersman says nobody on the island could tell him the king's name, only the size of him.
The cup goes to Ravn. Asked whether it is true, he says he did not say it was true; he said men landed on it. The lookout says the monks have the same fish in a book, and is not thanked.

The cup goes to the lookout, who had not expected it and spills some. Ravn says it is a good saying and would be better with a bigger bird. Nobody speaks for a while after that, and it is not a bad quiet.
That passed
The crew's heart is low and nobody is speaking. The lookout offers the one song he knows for it.
A grey evening at sea, the men slumped at their oars and not looking at one another; the lookout sitting upright in the bow with one hand a little raised, beginning to speak.
Nobody has said more than the stroke since yesterday. The bread is eaten without a word. It is the kind of quiet that ends with a man going ashore for good.

There is a song of a singer who lost his place to a better man. He counts over others who had it worse: a smith lamed, a woman wronged, a king shut thirty years in his fort. After each he says: that passed; so may this.
Hear it
Songs do not row: open a cask of the cargo's ale
A hard hour at the oars, and a plain word about where the next silver is
He says it through. After the second verse the men have the answer and say it with him, low, on the stroke: that passed; so may this. It is not cheerful. It is better than the quiet.
The bung is knocked out and the cup goes round until the cask rings hollow. By dark they are telling lies in three tongues. In the morning the cargo is a cask lighter and the stroke is together.

An hour's pull that leaves no breath for brooding, and then you say it plainly: where the cargo sells, what it should fetch, when they are paid. They have heard merchants before. But a named port is a thing to row toward.
Blows
The hand and the lookout are fighting between the thwarts. The steersman has a hand on each and is waiting for you.

Amidships in grey daylight: two young men locked together between the thwarts, one with a fistful of the other's hair; the steersman behind them with a hand on each man's collar, looking past them at the viewer.
It began over a wet cloak, or a word about a wet cloak. Now the hand has the lookout by the hair, the lookout has his teeth in the hand's wrist, and the boat is rocking.

By our law a grip on the hair is two shillings and a ducking is four, at three pennies to the shilling. The law prices what was done, not what was said. I can hold them until you choose, but not all day.
Part them: each pays the other's hurt from his share, as the law prices it
They finish it at the next landing: fists, no iron, the rest of you watching
One to the bow, one to the stern, and not a word
The hair is priced and the bite is priced, and it comes out that each owes the other six pennies. The steersman cuts both notches. They are too puzzled by the sum to go on being angry.
They let go. Each goes back to his oar with something to look forward to. The rowing is very good for some days, as each shows the other what he will be hitting.

One in the bow and one in the stern, with two men and four paces between them. They obey. They do not stop. The English have a saying that men do not quarrel who are not together; and a boat is together.
On the strand
The two who fought aboard are on the strand at the ebb to finish it. Half the landing has come down to watch.

A wide strand at low water with the wet sand shining: two men stripped to the waist circling each other; the crew and a ragged half-ring of townspeople and children watching; the boat aground behind them.
Low water, firm sand, and half the landing come down to watch. A man is already taking wagers in eggs.
Fists, no iron, and it stops when one of them sits down. I have their knives. If you want it stopped sooner, say so before the first blow and not after.
Let them
Stop it at first blood and make them drink from one cup (1 d)
Forbid it: not in front of a town the house trades in

It does not take long. The hand sits down first. The lookout pulls him up again, and they go to the alehouse with a black eye each and are not seen until dark, when they come back singing one song in two tongues.
The lookout goes down, and the hand kicks him as he lies. The mate is on them before the second kick. A rib is cracked, and what was a quarrel is now a debt.
First blood is the lookout's nose. You step between them and hold out one cup, a penny's worth of the landing's ale. Each must drink where the other drank. The watchers are disappointed and say so.
They put their shirts on again. The landing goes back up the strand, laughing at a boat whose master is afraid of a fist fight. Neither man thanks you, and each blames the other for it.
One of them goes
A knife was drawn in the night. The mate says the boat is too small for both men.
First light at a mooring: a bare knife lying on the middle thwart; the hand at one end of the boat and the lookout at the other, each with his back turned; the mate standing over the knife.
A knife was out in the night. Nobody was cut. I took it away, and I will not say whose it was, because by morning it would have been the other's.
The boat is seven paces long. On a ship of thirty oars I could keep them apart. Here one of them goes, or they swear it away before something they both fear.
Pay off the hand (6 d)
Pay off the lookout (6 d)
Keep both: each swears peace on the relics here, his hand in the other's
Six pennies and his bundle. He goes up the quay fast, to show he is not being sent. The lookout rows the next day as if he had won, and the day after as if he had not.
Six pennies and his bundle, with the waxed board on top. The hand watches him up the quay and then, for want of anything else to do, goes and sits in his place in the bow.

Each puts his right hand on the relics and his left in the other's, and says the words after the priest. The English say men do not quarrel who are not together. These two have sworn to be together and not quarrel, which is harder; and it holds.
Each swears with his hand on the relics. The hand looks at the lookout while he says it. The oath stops the knives. It does not stop anything else, and the boat is no longer than it was.
Six pennies light
Silver is missing from the purse. There are four men aboard and no door.
The stern of the boat by day: the merchant's purse open on the stern board, the coins laid out in rows with a gap in the last row; four men at their oars seen from behind, none of them turning round.
The purse was counted at the last landing and it is counted again now. Six pennies light. There are four men aboard, no door, no lock, and no stranger has put a foot over the gunwale.
I will not name a man on a guess. I say only that all four of us can count to six, and that I would rather be searched than wondered about.
Turn out every bundle now, your own first
Say nothing, nick the edge of every coin left, and watch
Tell them the next loss comes out of every share alike
Bundles are tipped out on the thwarts, yours first. Six pennies lie in the toe of a spare shoe. Everyone now knows whose shoe, and everyone has had his own poor things looked at to learn it.
Bundles are tipped out on the thwarts, yours first. Combs, a spare shirt, a wooden cross, a hammer cast in lead. No silver. Four men have been searched like thieves, and three of them were not.
You say nothing. That night you nick the rim of every penny that is left with the point of your knife, the way silver is tested in the north, and put the purse back where it was.
They hear it in silence. Three men look at a fourth, but not all at the same one. The purse stays whole for the season. Each man sleeps with one eye on the others, which is cheaper than a lock.
The nicked penny
The missing silver has been traced to the hand. He does not deny it.
A quay at dusk: the merchant holds a single penny up to the last light, a notch showing in its rim; the hand stands before him with his arms hanging and his head down; the mate a step behind.
A penny with a nick in its rim has come back to you in change from an ale-wife at the landing. She remembers who paid her with it.
The six pennies lay in the toe of his spare shoe. He has had some days at his oar to think what to say.
I took it. My brother stood surety for a neighbour's cow and the cow died, and they come for the surety at Martinmas. I meant to put it back out of my share. Every thief says that. I know.
He has pulled his weight since the first day. That is all I can say for him, and I have said it.
Put him ashore at the next landing with what he is owed, less the six
He pays it back twice over from his share, and keeps his oar
Ask what the debt is, and lend him the six against his season's share

At the next landing he is paid to the day, less six, and goes up the strand without looking round. The men are easier. A thief put ashore is talked of in every boat-shed on the coast, and so is the master who did it.
Twelve pennies are cut from his tally. He rows the rest of the season for almost nothing, and does it without a word. He has kept his oar. He does not mistake that for being forgiven.

Six pennies, lent this time, with a notch cut against his season. For a moment he cannot speak. The cow is paid for at Martinmas, and you have a hand who would row you to the world's edge and back for bread.
Six pennies, lent this time. He thanks you with wet eyes, and is gone from the next landing before light with the six, the first six and the mate's good whetstone.
One cloak
The hand and Ravn have become friends. It changes how the watches fall.
A night watch at sea under a clear sky: two men, one grey-fair and lean, one young, sitting shoulder to shoulder in the bow under a single cloak, a fishing line running out between them.
It began with a shared cloak on a wet watch. Now the hand cuts Ravn's bread and Ravn mends the hand's shoes, and they have a plan about a net.
He talks too much and knows nothing, and I like him. Put us on one watch, if you can.
Put them on one watch for the season
Advance them three pennies between them for the net they want (3 d)
Keep them on separate watches: friends talk more than they pull

They take the dark watch together for the season. The boat is better looked after between midnight and dawn than at any other hour. Once Ravn is heard to say, as if to the sea: 'Rich did I feel when a comrade I found, for man is man's delight.'
Three pennies buy twine, and the net grows on the thwart between them all that month: a Danish mesh on a Frisian headrope. The first herring out of it are given to you, cooked.

They take it without argument and change watches as they are told. For a week each gives up half his sleep to sit through half the other's watch. Then they tire, as you knew they would, and are only shipmates again.
A gift looks for a gift
Ravn has given the hand a thing he made. The hand has nothing to give back, and comes to you.
The boat at rest in soft light: the hand turns over in his fingers a small bone needle-case carved with a beast biting its own back; the Dane, further off, pretends to be busy with a rope.
Ravn has carved a needle-case from a sheep's shank, with a beast on it that bites its own back, and put it in the hand's bundle without a word.
Among his people a gift looks for a gift. Everybody knows that. I have a knife, which I need, and a tally, which you hold. I cannot give him a notch.
Advance him four pennies on his share (4 d)
Let him have one antler comb from the cargo, on his tally (1 d)
Tell him a gift owed is no shame before Yule
Four pennies against his share. At the next landing he buys a bronze cloak-pin, plain and heavy. Ravn looks at it a long moment and puts it on, and is not seen without it again.

An antler comb from the cargo, and a penny on his tally. Ravn runs his thumb along the teeth and says his people's verse for it: 'Gift-givers' friendships are longest found, if fair their fates may be.' He combs his beard for the first time this voyage.
He nods, not much comforted. He will owe it until midwinter and think about it every day until then, which is perhaps what a gift is for.
Counting in his tongue
Ravn is teaching the hand his tongue, a word to each stroke of the oar. You could learn it with him.
Two men on one oar bench in sunlight, the Dane holding up his fingers one at a time as he pulls, the hand's mouth open, repeating; the wake curling behind the boat.
One, two, three, on the pull, in Ravn's tongue. The hand says them after him and gets the fourth wrong every time. It is nearly his own counting, and then suddenly it is not.
One to ten is the same road as yours with different mud on it, and after ten we part. Learn what a thing costs, and the word for too much. The rest is for poets.
Take the oar beside them and learn it too
Let them be: a hand who can ask a price in the north is worth his bread
Tell them to count in their heads

By the end of the watch you can count to a hundred, ask what a thing costs, and say that it is too much. Ravn says you sound like a Frisian with a cold. He says it in his own tongue, and you follow him.
The hand counts strokes in Danish all afternoon and reaches forty before the others threaten him. Ravn corrects him without turning his head.
The counting stops. The oars are quieter. So are the men, and the afternoon is the longer for it.
How to refuse in his tongue
You can count and ask a price in Ravn's tongue. He offers the next lesson.
The Dane and the merchant face to face across the cargo, the Dane with a penny lying in one palm and the other hand pushing it away, his eyebrows raised: a lesson in refusing.
You can ask a price. Now learn to hear one and look sad. Then you say that's too much, and that's still too much, and then your last word. A man needs three last words.
At Sliesthorp, the Danes' market on the Schlei, a stranger who bargains in their tongue is cheated by a smaller measure than one who points.
Learn the market words
Ask instead for what a guest says at a hall door
Enough for one voyage
Too much, still too much, my last word, weigh it again, and the names of nine goods. He makes you say each until he stops wincing. It is a merchant's Danish: no poetry in it, and worth more.

He gives you what is said at a hall door in the old verse: 'Hail to the giver! a guest has come; where shall the stranger sit?' The rest of the verse, he says, is about being quick with a sword. You can have that another time.
He shrugs. The words will keep, he says. They have kept this long.
Bread, butter and cheese
The English lookout and the Frisian steersman have found how near their tongues lie. It is a thing a merchant can use.
The steersman and the lookout sitting on the cargo with a loaf, a pat of butter on a leaf and a wedge of cheese laid out between them, each man pointing at the cheese.
The lookout pointed at the food and said three words in English. The steersman said three in Frisian. They were very nearly the same three, and both men looked insulted.
Bread, butter, cheese. Cow, boat, water, day. He says them the way my grandmother did. It is like hearing my own tongue through a wall.
It is our tongue with the edges worn off. They took it over the sea with them and left it out in the rain.
Have the lookout give you the English for every thing in the hold
Ask him what an English reeve says when a foreign boat lands
Leave them to it
Cloth, wine, quern, comb, pot, salt, and what is good and bad in each. By landfall you can praise your own cargo and doubt another man's in English, which is the whole of trade.

He gives you the reeve's questions: whose man are you, what do you carry, who knows you here. And the old Kentish law behind them: a man buying in Lundenwic has two or three true men for witness, or the king's wic-reeve. Have your witnesses' names ready, he says, before you have your goods out.
They go on through the animals and reach the weather. Whatever else happens to the boat, two of her men will be able to complain to each other.
Twenty-three marks
The lookout is showing the mate his letters on a waxed board. There is room on the thwart for a third.
A calm bright day at sea: the lookout holds a small waxed tablet on his knee and scratches at it with a stylus; the big mate bends close over it, frowning, a thick finger hovering over one mark.

A waxed board the size of a hand, and a pointed stick. The lookout cuts a mark, says its sound, smooths the wax with his thumb and cuts the next. Twenty-three of them, he says, and every book in the world.
A is two rafters and a tie-beam, if that helps. It helped me. The brothers beat it into us with a psalm; I thought I would try it without the beating.
A man's name can be written on a list, and the list sent a long way south. I want to know what my own looks like. Then I can look for one that is near it.
Sit down by the mate and learn them too
Have him cut your own name and the boat's
Leave them to it

You get as far as M before the light goes. The mate gets to F and stays there, cutting it over and over with a hand made for an oar. The lookout says both of you are quicker than the boys were. He is a kind liar.
He cuts your name, and under it the boat's. You copy them until the wax is too scored to hold a line. A few marks, and they are you. It is strange how little there is of it.
The lesson goes on behind you. By evening the mate can cut his own name, and is looking at it as a man looks at his own footprint.
Sixteen staves
Ravn is cutting his people's letters into the edge of a thwart with his knife.
Close on the edge of a thwart: a knife point cutting a row of straight-stroked staves into the wood, the Dane's scarred hand on the knife; shavings curling, sea light behind.
Straight cuts only, down and slantwise, never along the grain, where a line would be lost. Sixteen staves. He says his grandfather's row had more, and that nobody misses them.

This one's cattle. Wealth, I mean. It comes first, so somebody knew what men want. This one's the god, and this one's ice. One stave, several sounds. You must know what the man meant before you can read what he cut.
Have him say each one, and cut them yourself beside his
Have him cut the boat's name where the toll man will not look
Tell him to cut his lessons on a stick, not on the boat
You cut all sixteen beside his. Yours lean. He says leaning staves can still be read, as a drunk man can still be understood, and makes you cut them again.
Under the stern board, where no toll man puts his hand, he cuts the boat's name, and after it a few staves he does not explain. Asked, he says they are so that she knows who she is in the dark.
He looks at the thwart, then at you, and puts the knife away. A boat is wood, he says, and wood is what staves are for. But he cuts no more on yours.
A riddle in the fog
Fog, and nothing to do but listen. Ravn asks a riddle to keep the men from hearing things.

Thick white fog, the boat a dim shape with her stem vanishing into it; the men sitting very still with their heads cocked to listen; only the Dane has his face turned to the viewer, and he is speaking.
Fog so thick that the stem has gone. Every sound is the wrong size. The hand has twice heard surf where there is none, and the steersman is listening so hard it hurts to watch.
'Who is the huge one, who passes over the earth, swallowing water and woods; he fears the wind, but no man, and wages war on the sun?'
Don't look at me. I give the questions. The answers are a man's own work.
Take the riddle
Tell him to listen for surf
You take it. The men argue over it in whispers for an hour, which is an hour they do not spend hearing rocks. Ravn listens to every wrong answer with great courtesy.
He listens for surf. So does everyone else, and each man hears it somewhere different.
A riddle at dawn
Dawn at anchor. Everything aboard is wet and it has not rained. Ravn has a riddle.
Dawn at anchor in summer: every rope and thwart beaded with drops under a low red sun; the Dane licking the back of his own wet hand and looking sideways at the merchant.
First light. The sail, the thwarts, the men's hair: all wet, and not a cloud all night.
'What drink was it I drank yesterday; it was neither wine nor water, nor mead, nor beer, nor aught of meat kind; yet I went thirstless away?'
Take the riddle
Not before bread
You take it with you into the day. Ravn wrings his cloak out over the side with unusual care, and says nothing more about drink.
He agrees that bread comes first, and that a riddle keeps better than bread does.
A riddle at anchor
The boat lies to her anchor and the lookout remembers a riddle the monks made.
The boat riding to a taut anchor rope in a tideway at evening; the lookout leaning over the bow and looking down along the rope into green water.
The brothers made riddles in the evenings, when they should have been silent. One begins: 'Oft with the wave I must contend, and against the wind fight.' It ends: 'Say what I am call'd.'
'I am strong in the strife, if I am still.' I never had the answer at school. I had never been in a boat.
Take the riddle
Ask whether the monks made any that were less holy
He says it through and you keep it. He watches you as his masters must have watched him, and enjoys it more than he should.
He goes red to the ears. There is one about an onion, he says, and one about a key, and he was beaten for knowing both. He gives you the holy one. The men ask about the onion all evening.
A riddle after the squall
A squall has gone through and left hail in the bilge. Ravn has a riddle.

Just after a squall: a ragged black cloud going away over the sea with the sun breaking under it; white hailstones lying in the bilge and on the cargo; the Dane holding one up between finger and thumb.
The squall has gone through like a cart over a bridge. There is hail in the bilge the size of peas, and the sail is steaming.
'What was that wonder: the white flyers beat the rock, while the black ones are embedded in the sand?'
Take the riddle
Bail first
You take it. Ravn drops his hailstone into the bilge and watches it go, as if it had said its part.
They bail. The hail goes over the side with the water, and the riddle with it, for now.
A riddle on a fair wind
She is running well. Ravn has a riddle for the watch.
The boat heeling under a full sail on a bright blowing day, spray off her bow; the Dane at the sheet, looking up into the belly of the sail.
A fair wind on the quarter and the sail as hard as a board. She has not gone like this since the spring. Nobody is rowing, and everybody is pleased with himself.
'Whence comes the wind that fares o'er the waves yet never itself is seen?'
A god asked a giant that, with a head staked on the answering. I only ask for sport, so keep your head.
Take the riddle
From the south-west: ask the sail
You take it. He nods and goes back to the sheet. The wind does not say.
He allows that the sail knows where it comes from today. Where it comes from at all, he says, is another road, and he will leave you on it.
A riddle with no wind in it
Becalmed. Ravn gives five names for one thing and asks what men call it.
A becalmed evening sea like poured metal with the sail slack; the Dane counting on the five fingers of one hand, held up against a huge low sun.
The gods call it 'The Quiet', the Wanes 'The Hush of the Winds', the giants 'The Sultry', the elves 'Day's Stillness', the dwarfs 'The Shelter of Day'.
That's five names. Men have a sixth, a short one, and you're sitting in it.
Take the riddle
I call it a day's pay gone
You take it. The sail hangs. Ravn looks content, as a man does who has found the one use for a day like this.
He considers it, and says the dwarfs would like that name; they count too. But it is not the one in the verse.
The answer
You have the answer to one of Ravn's riddles. He has been waiting to see how long it would take.

The Dane and the merchant seated facing each other on the thwarts, the merchant leaning forward and speaking, the Dane with his head on one side and one eyebrow up; the other men pretending not to listen.
You've the look of a man with something in his mouth that isn't bread. Say it!
He has not asked once since he set it. He has counted the days, though, and can tell you how many.
Give him your answer
Answer, and set him one of your own
You say it. He lets a breath go by, then nods once, as a man nods at a knot that holds. He sets you the next before you have finished being pleased.

You answer his, and set him one of your own. He begins three answers and stops each. At last he laughs aloud, which nobody aboard has heard before, and says he will have it by Yule. By nightfall he is asking the others.
You answer his, and set him one of your own. He has yours before you have done saying it; his grandmother asked it, he says, of the goats. But he is pleased to have been asked.
A rune stick
There is a rune-cut stick in the chest that you cannot read. Ravn can, and will do some of it.
The Dane holds a flat stick cut with runes close to his eyes and turns it to the low light; the merchant at his shoulder; the open chest at their feet.
Give it here. This is a man's name. This is 'owns'. The next stave could be any of three sounds, so I'll say all three, and you tell me which makes a word. That's all reading is.
In the short row one stave serves for several sounds. A reader must guess the word to read the word, and the man who cut it knew that and did not care.
Let him read his part, and work out the rest
Ask him to read all of it
Read it yourself, stave by stave
He says the sounds; you find the words. A name, then 'owns', then, after some false starts, the thing owned. He grunts each time you have one before he does.
He reads it off like a man counting sheep and hands it back. Now you know what it says. You do not know how it says it, and he seems to think you have had the worse of the bargain.

It takes you from noon to the evening meal, stave by stave, saying each of its sounds under your breath. Ravn watches and keeps his mouth shut until you have it. Then he cannot keep it shut any longer.
A Latin leaf
There is a leaf of Latin in the chest that you cannot read. The lookout can read some of it.
The lookout with a single parchment leaf held flat on his knee against the wind, his finger under a line and his lips moving; the merchant looking over his arm.
It is a clear hand. 'In the name of': that I have. Then a name. Then a word I ought to know, and my master would have beaten me for.
I read slowly, but I do not read wrong. If you take every third word and I take the rest, we shall both have learned something by the foot of the leaf.
Have him read what he can, and puzzle out the rest with him
Ask him only to tell you what it says
Put it back in the chest till a monk is aboard
A word from him, a word from you, a quarrel over an ending. By the foot of the leaf you know what it says, and three words you will know again when you meet them.
He reads it to himself with his lips moving, and tells you the sense of it in a breath. It was quicker. He looks a little sorry, like a man asked for the fish and not the fishing.
The leaf goes back between its boards. Parchment keeps. So does not knowing.
A boy by the mooring post
The boat is a man short. A farmer's younger son asks for the empty oar.

A mooring post on a Frisian quay in morning light: a lanky boy of sixteen standing very straight beside it, barefoot, with a bundle on a stick; the mate looking him up and down; one oar lying unused in the boat.
He has been standing by the mooring post since before light, so as to be seen being early. Big hands, bare feet, and a bundle that is mostly cheese.
My brother has the farm and the cows, and I have what is left, which is me. I can row. I have rowed the dung boat every spring since I could lift the oar.
He has the shoulders. He has never been out of sight of his own mound. Half a wage until he stops being sick over the side: that is fair, and he knows it.
Take him at a boy's wage till Martinmas
Take him at a man's wage from the first day, with hand-money (2 d)
Tell him to come back with a beard

A boy's wage till Martinmas, and a handclasp. He is sick before the river mouth and rowing again before he has finished. The mate pretends not to be counting the days until the boy has earned the other half.
Two pennies of hand-money and a man's wage from the first stroke. He looks at the pennies as if they might be taken back. He is as sick as any boy, and rows like a man who has been bought dear.
He takes it standing straight, says he will be at this post next spring with the beard, and walks to the next boat down.
A Dane mending nets
The boat is a man short. A Dane whose ship went home without him is looking for an oar.
A net-drying rack on a quay: a lean, grey-fair man sits under it mending a net with a bone needle, a sea-chest beside him; the steersman stands a little way off with his arms crossed.
He sits under the net racks mending another man's net for his bread. A sea-chest, a good knife, and hands that have held an oar for thirty years. He does not look up until you stop.
My ship went home. I was ashore; it does not matter why. I row, steer and splice, and I know the waters north of here better than your steersman knows his wife. I eat what is given.
A Dane, after what was done on the holy island. He may be an honest man. I would want to know which ship he came in, and he will not say.
He is a heathen and he will pour ale over my stem. I say that first. I say second that he is the best oar on this quay, and I have looked.
Hire him
Hire him if he will let a priest sign him with the cross first
Not this season
He puts his chest under the third thwart and takes the oar as if he had left it there yesterday. The steersman crosses himself, and then shows him where the bailer is kept.

He hears what is wanted and shrugs: a thumb and some words. The priest signs him on the forehead and the breast, and he steps aboard neither a Christian nor quite the other thing. The steersman is content. The Dane counts it as part of the wage.
He nods and goes back to the net. The steersman breathes out. The oar stays empty, and the best pair of hands on the quay is left sitting under a rack.
Twelve oars for the Seine
The master of a bigger ship wants your hand, and says so in front of you.

A busy emporium waterfront: a broad ship of twelve oars lying alongside, her well-dressed master standing on the quay with his thumbs in his belt, talking to the hand; the merchant's small boat in the foreground.
Twelve oars, bound for the Seine and wine. I give a penny every three days, and meat twice in the week. I say it in front of you, master, so that nobody can call it stealing.
It is a better wage and a drier ship. I gave you my word till Martinmas. I am telling you what was said to me. I have not said yes.
Match it (8 d)
Let him go, paid to the day, and shake the skipper's hand (6 d)
Hold him to his word till Martinmas
Eight pennies now, and the big ship's terms. He stays. The skipper laughs and says a small boat that pays like a great one will soon be neither.
Paid to the day, and your hand to the skipper. He says he will remember a master who lets a man better himself; at sea that is a debt. The hand looks back twice from the big ship's bow.
He looks at the big ship, and at you, and says a word is a word. He rows on. Now and then, on fast days, he mentions meat.
He says a word is a word. In the morning the big ship has gone on the ebb and so has he. His oar is left shipped, and his tally stick laid across it with the notches he has given up.
A roof that wants a man
The hand is leaving the sea to marry a widow with a boat-shed. He is telling you, not asking.
An autumn day at a Frisian landing: the hand in a clean shirt stands on the quay beside a sturdy woman of thirty with keys at her belt; behind them a boat-shed with a net hung up to dry.

She has a house on the mound, a boat-shed, four cows, and her man two years under the turf. She needs somebody to mend the roof, and I need a roof. We are agreed. I am telling you before the priest does.
A widow in this country holds her dead husband's house and gives or keeps it in her own name. He is marrying upward, and knows it.
Pay him to the day, and a bolt of good cloth for the bride (6 d)
Pay him to the day and wish him cows (6 d)
Ask him for one more season, at a share and not a wage

Six pennies, and a bolt of the good cloth carried up the mound on the mate's shoulder. The bride feels the weave, and says her husband's old master may tie up at her shed whenever he passes. On this coast that is worth more than the bolt.
Paid to the day, and you wish him cows. He wishes you wind. He goes up the mound without his sea-walk for the first time; he has been practising.
A share and not a wage: he works the sum, and then she works it, faster. One more season, she says, and he comes home at Martinmas with silver or not at all. He takes his oar.
He hears you out and shakes his head. She would wait, he says. He is not sure the roof would. You pay him to the day.
Up the strand
The season is over. The boat comes out of the water, and the steersman wants her seams done while she is dry.
A November strand under low cloud: the boat hauled up on log rollers and propped with stakes, her hull dark and wet; the steersman runs his thumb along a seam; a tar pot smokes over a small fire.
She comes up the strand on rollers with eight men on the rope, and sits there looking twice the size and half as clever. Weed to the third strake.

She has wept along the keel since Lammas. Dry her, rake out the old stuffing, tarred moss into every seam, and a coat over all. Do it now and she is tight at Easter. Leave it and we bail our way to England.
Haul her and do it now: tar, moss and the strand's men (8 d)
Haul her and broach the tar in the hold (3 d for moss and rollers)
Haul her, and leave the tar till spring
Three days of scraping, stuffing and hot tar. The whole strand smells of it. When it is done the steersman walks round her once and says nothing, and she shines black like a wet seal.

The cargo's own tar is broached and a part of it goes on her. What is left will sell short, and the buyer will say so. But she is tight, and the steersman has tar to the elbows and a face like a feast day.
She is propped and left. The steersman looks at that seam each time he passes, the way a man looks at a tooth he knows will have to come out.
Four men and three months of dark
The boat is laid up. The men must sleep and eat somewhere until the sea opens.

Inside a long low house by firelight: a hearth down the middle, benches along the walls, the host standing with a ladle; the four crewmen in the doorway with their bundles and snow on their shoulders.

Four men till Candlemas: a place by the fire, pottage twice a day, ale on feast days. A penny a man a week. I answer for you to the lord's man while you are under my roof, so you will give me nothing to answer for.
The boat-shed is four pennies, and no walls to speak of. Men winter in worse. They do not come out of it in spring the men they went in.
A guest should be gone before the host counts his logs, and a quarter of the year's a long time to sit at another man's fire.
The host's fire till Candlemas (16 d)
The boat-shed and a fire-pit (4 d)
