Send each man to his own hearth till the geese go north

Sixteen pennies. The men sleep dry and wake fed, and by Candlemas they are fat, quarrelsome and well. On the last night Ravn gives the host his verse as a parting gift: 'Love becomes loathing if long one sits by the hearth in another's home.' The host takes it for thanks.
A fire-pit in the lee of the propped hull, and hides hung for walls. They live. The cough goes round all four twice, and by the end they speak of the host's house as of a king's hall.
Each man takes his bundle and his road. The mate goes last and asks what day you want them back. When the geese go north, you say. He says geese are not all of one mind.
Long nights
Midwinter ashore. The men have nothing to do, and the mate wants them given something.
The lodging by night in midwinter: men sprawled on the benches round a low fire, one whittling, one asleep with his mouth open; through the gap of the door, snow and a dark blue afternoon.
It is dark by the ninth hour, and dark again whenever anyone wakes. The men have mended everything that could be mended, and have begun to mend things that were whole.
Give them work or give them a reason. Yesterday two of them fell out over whose turn it was to fetch water, and neither of them wanted water.
Set them to lay rope from the hemp in the hold
Let the lookout teach letters by the fire to whoever will sit
Stand them an evening at the alehouse and say nothing of work (3 d)

The hemp is combed, spun and laid up in three strands, with the whole length of the lodging for a ropewalk and the host's children turning the top. By the thaw there is a coil of new rope, worth twice the bundle.
The lookout cuts letters in the hearth ash with a stick, and whoever will sit, sits. You are there most evenings. So is the mate. So, before long, is the host's daughter, which was not the plan.
Three pennies of the alehouse's best, and not a word about work. They come back arm in arm through the snow, one of them carried. The morning is very quiet.
Midwinter
Christmas. The church is full. Ravn has a fire of his own behind the boat-shed and has asked nobody.

Midwinter night with snow on the ground: on the left a small wooden church, its door open, candlelight and people inside; on the right, behind a boat-shed, the Dane alone at a fire of his own with a horn of ale; the boat on her props between the two lights.
The church is full to the door and breathing out candle-smoke. Behind the boat-shed there is a second light, lower and redder, with one man sitting at it.
Tonight the year turns. My people drink to it, and to the dead. I've ale and a fire. I'll ask nobody, so nobody need say no.
Bede wrote that our own forefathers kept this very night, before the faith came: the mothers' night, they called it. He does not say what they did. I think it was probably this.
Mass first. After that, where a man sits is between him and his stomach. But mass first.
Mass with the Christians, then Ravn's fire with all of them (3 d for ale)
Mass, and the host's table after
Go and sit at his fire now

Mass, standing, with the whole landing. Then ale is carried round behind the shed, where Ravn moves over without a word. He drinks to the year and to his dead. The others, after a moment, drink to theirs. They are not different dead.
Mass, and the host's table after, with a goose. It is warm and loud. Once, when the door opens, the smaller fire can be seen beyond the shed, burning low, and the same one man at it.

You sit down across the fire from him. He fills the horn and hands it over as if he had expected you. The bell rings for mass behind your back. In the morning the steersman wishes you the joy of the feast, correctly, and nothing more.
Three men by the boat
The sea is opening. Of the men sent home for the winter, one has not come back.
A raw spring morning on the strand: the boat fresh-tarred on her rollers, ready to go down; three men standing by her with their bundles, and room beside them for a fourth; a skein of geese overhead.
The geese went north four days ago. Three men stand by the boat with their bundles. The mate has counted them twice, as if that might help.
The hand is not come. His cousin is here with the eel boats, and says the father is worse and the boy is torn. He did not say he is not coming. He did not say he is.
Wait a week for him
Send his cousin back with hand-money and a day named (2 d)
Sail a man short and hire at the first landing

On the sixth day he comes along the dyke at a run with his bundle bouncing, shouting that he is here before anyone can hear him. He buried his father three days ago. He takes his oar and does not speak of it.
A week of fair wind blows itself out over an idle boat. He does not come. On the eighth morning the cousin brings word: the farm cannot spare him. You have lost the week and the man.
Two pennies and a named day go back with the cousin. Hand-money taken is a hiring made. He is on the strand the evening before the day, a little ashamed, with his mother's blessing and a cheese.
Three men and an empty thwart go down the rollers on the tide. She steers a little crooked with the odd oar. The mate says nothing about it at every stroke.
Three kinds of silver
The purse is tipped out to be counted. Ravn and the steersman do not agree on what is in it.

Close on the stern board: a purse spilled out, of small thick pennies with a king's name, broad thin coins covered in flowing script, and chopped pieces of ring and rod; the Dane's knife point testing one piece, the steersman's finger pressed on a penny.
Tipped out on the stern board: the king's pennies; broader, thinner coins out of the east with writing like worm-tracks; and silver that was never coin at all, rings and rods chopped to a weight.
A stamp is a king saying trust me. I trust the knife. Cut it, bend it, weigh it. Silver doesn't lie, and I've known kings who did.
The king's penny passes by count from here to Rome, and nobody has to bite it. That scrap is thieves' leavings, and the worm-writing may be a curse, for all you know.
Reckon it Ravn's way: all of it by weight
Reckon it the steersman's way: the king's penny, and the rest at what a moneyer gives
Reckon it both ways and believe the smaller

Everything goes into the pan against the lead weights, pennies and scrap alike. It comes to a little more than the steersman's count. He says a pan can be made to say anything, and watches it closely ever after.

The pennies are told off by tens; the rest is set aside for a moneyer, who will take his cut. It comes to a little less. Ravn picks an eastern coin out of the heap, looks at the writing, and says somebody thought that worth saying on silver.
Counted, and then weighed. The two sums differ by four pennies, and you cut the smaller on the tally. Each man is satisfied that his was the way that caught the other's mistake.
Iron under the ballast
There are blades in the hold that the king's law forbids. The steersman wants it said aloud.
The boat under way in dull weather, the ballast stones amidships shifted to show a long bundle wrapped in oiled hide; the steersman at his oar staring at it; the other men looking anywhere else.
There are blades under the ballast. I say it aloud once, so that nobody aboard can swear he did not know. The king's law forbids them over the border, and a toll man reads cargo for his living.
The king has made it death now, at Pitres: sell arms to the Northmen and you hang. I steer this boat. I will not steer her to a gallows.
They forbid it because they fear the edge coming back, and that tells you what the edge is worth in the north. I know who buys. I'd sooner not say.
The king calls my people his enemies whenever it suits him. I would arm anyone he calls an enemy. But I would want paying for it.
A double share this voyage for every man, for the risk (12 d)
Give your word that this is the last such cargo
Tell him his work is the steering oar
Twelve pennies: a double share to each man for the voyage. The steersman takes his, and says he has now been paid to be hanged, which is more than most men get.
You give your word. The steersman holds you in his eye a moment, and nods. He steers for the toll as if he carried eggs. He will remember what you said, and the day you said it.
He closes his mouth and steers. He steers very well. At the next toll he looks straight ahead and leaves every word of the talking to you.
Where the book rides
There is a book in the cargo. The lookout says there is no dry place aboard, and asks to read from it.
The lookout kneeling in the bow with a thick book in a leather wrapper held against his chest like a child, spray flying past him; his open sea-chest beside him, lined with waxed cloth.
There is no dry place in this boat. I have looked. A wet book swells, the ink runs, the leaves stick together, and what took a brother two winters to write is a brick of glue.
It would ride best in my chest, in waxed cloth. And at anchor, with dry hands... I have not had a book open in front of me since I left. I would be careful. I would only read.
It rides in his sea-chest, wrapped in waxed cloth, and stays shut
It rides in his chest, and he may read aloud from it at anchor
Under the stern boards with the silver
It rides in his chest in three wraps of waxed cloth, and comes out at the journey's end as dry as the day it was bound. He never opened it. He tells you so twice.
A sea comes over the quarter in the night, and his chest is found on its side, afloat in the bilge. The cloth held at five edges of six. The book is opened at the landing and will not close again.

At anchor, with his hands washed and dried, he reads aloud under the sail: the Latin first, then the sense of it. The men listen as they listen to weather. When he closes it he wraps it like a child. There is not a spot on it.

At anchor he is reading aloud, the book open on his knees, when the boat swings to the tide and a wave slaps in over the bow. He throws himself across the page. It is not enough. He does not speak that day or the next.
It rides under the stern boards beside the silver, and by luck the bilge stays low. It arrives dry. The lookout looks under the boards each morning, as a man looks in on a sleeping child.
Under the stern boards is where the bilge water runs when she heels. When the boards are lifted at the landing the book lies in two fingers of black water. The silver beside it has taken no harm.
Ships in the north
Every boat from the north has news of the Danish king's fleet. Two of your men have reasons to care.
Two boats lying gunwale to gunwale at sea to trade news, a man in the other boat pointing north; in the near boat the Dane looks down at his hands and the steersman stares away northward.

Every boat out of the north tells it larger: the Danes' king has a fleet at sea; he has broken a market on the Wendish coast and carried its merchants off; and nobody will say where the ships turn next.
I know men in those ships. Good oars. A fleet that size is not launched to look at the weather.
My mother's people are on the islands. Low sand, no wall, and no count nearer than a day. If that many ships want silver, that is where it lies nearest the water.
Ask Ravn what a fleet that size is for
Promise the steersman a call at the islands before the summer is out
Say nothing: news that large arrives by itself

He takes a long time. A fleet is for being paid, he says: in silver, or in what the silver would have bought. He will not say more. He has said it to you and not to the steersman, and you are meant to notice that.
You give him your word: the islands, before the summer is out. He thanks you shortly, and steers. That evening he is heard counting his kin over, house by house, the way other men pray.
You say nothing, and the news goes on arriving with every boat you meet, each time a little larger. Both men listen to all of it, and neither looks at the other.
Go or wait
A stiff wind at the mooring. The steersman wants to wait a tide, the lookout wants to go, and the mate counts the bread.
A mooring in a stiff wind, the boat snatching at her ropes, whitecaps beyond the harbour mouth; the steersman pointing at the swell, the lookout pointing out to sea, the mate holding up a bread sack.
There is a swell running in that this wind did not make, and the gulls went inland at noon. Something larger is behind it. I would wait a tide.
It is fair for where we are going, and it will not be fairer. Half the boats here have gone already. We are sitting on a fair wind as a hen sits on a stone.
Bread for five days. A tide costs half a day. I do not say go or stay. I say what is in the sack.
Go now
Wait a tide
Take the steersman aside and ask what he sees coming

She goes out through the harbour mouth with a rush, and the lookout whoops. The steersman takes her over the bar without a word. It is as the English churl said from the boar's back: now it is in the pig's judgement.
The boat stays on her ropes, and the men find things to do with them. Other masts go out past the point. The lookout watches each one out of sight. The steersman watches the gulls.
Away from the others he says what he sees: which way the swell sets, what the sky did at dawn, what he would do if the boat were his. He is seldom wrong, and he likes being asked.
The evening song: Scyld
Evening at sea. The lookout says he has a long song by heart, and offers the first part of it.

A ship with a ring-carved stem pushed out from a winter shore with no one at her oars: a dead king laid by the mast, weapons and gold heaped on him, a gold banner set over his head; mourners standing on the beach.
I have a song by heart, a long one: a king, a monster in a hall, and at the end a dragon. One part an evening would see us through a summer.
It begins with a king of the Danes who came from the sea as a child, nobody's son, and went back to it dead, in a ship full of treasure. No man knows who unloaded her.
Fog round the boat. His voice does not carry past the stem, and it is the only thing out there that is where it seems to be.
Listen
Ask where he had it, then listen
Not tonight
He says the part through in his own tongue, on a beat the steersman finds himself keeping with the oar. The words are in your chest now, to go over again by daylight.

An old brother at the monastery had been a king's man before he took his vows, he says, and said it over to the boys in the dark when the abbot slept. He was beaten for learning it and has never been sorry. Then he begins.
He nods and keeps it for another evening. A song that long has learned to wait.
The evening song: Heorot
Evening at sea. The lookout has the next part of his song ready, if you want it.
A huge gabled timber hall on a rise, lit from within, with antlers on its gable ends and a harper seen through the open door; far off on a dark moor, a hunched shape listening.
The Danes build the greatest hall there ever was, with horns on its gables, and the harp is heard in it every night. Out on the moor something hears it too, and hates the sound.
No wind. The sea is so still that every word lies on it.
The evening song: Grendel
Inside the hall at night: warriors asleep on the benches by a dying fire; a great clawed shadow filling the doorway.
Grendel comes while they sleep and carries off thirty men. Then again the next night. For twelve winters the best hall in the world stands empty after dark, and the king can do nothing.
It is blowing, and he has to say it loud. That suits some parts.
The evening song: the Geats put to sea
A ship with foam at her stem run up on a shingle beach below cliffs; fifteen armed men stepping ashore; a single rider coming down the cliff path with his spear raised.

Over the sea a young man of the Geats hears of it. He picks fourteen men and a ship. They sail a day and a night, and a watchman rides down to the strand and asks them, very civilly, who they think they are.
The evening song: the coast-warden
On the cliff top: the young leader speaking with open hands to the mounted coast-warden; behind them a stone-paved road running inland to the far gold roof of the hall.
He gives the coast-warden his father's name and his errand. The warden says a sharp man must judge words as well as deeds, and sets a guard on their ship. I thought of our toll man.
The evening song: at the hall door
Shields leaned in a row against the wall of the hall, and spears stacked together like a grove of ash; the Geats sitting on a bench by the door while a door-keeper goes in.
They stack their shields against the wall and sit down on the bench outside, and a door-keeper goes in to ask whether the king will see them. Even in a song, a man waits at a door.
The evening song: Hrothgar and Beowulf
The high seat of the hall: a white-haired king leaning forward, the young man standing before him in mail with his bare hands held out and open.
The king knew his father. And the young man says he will meet the thing with his bare hands, since it carries no sword. If he loses, he says, nobody will have the trouble of burying him.
The evening song: a feud paid for
The feast bench: the old king with a cup in his hand, telling a story; small in a corner of the picture, a ship carrying a chest of treasure over the sea.

The old king tells how the young man's father once killed a man and began a feud, and how the king ended it by sending treasure over the sea. So the son's coming is a debt paid, though nobody says so.
The evening song: Unferth
A sneering man seated at the king's feet with a cup, pointing up across the fire at the young stranger; faces along the benches turned to see what he will answer.
A man at the king's feet, Unferth, has drunk enough to be jealous. He asks whether this is the same Beowulf who swam against Breca for a boast, seven nights in the winter sea, and lost.
The evening song: the sea-beasts
Under green water at night: a swimmer in mail with a sword in his hand, a toothed sea-beast locked on him and others circling; far above, the surface and a storm.

He answers that he did not lose. Sea-beasts dragged him to the bottom and he killed nine of them, and the sea put him ashore among the Finns. Then he tells Unferth what he thinks of a man who has killed only his own brothers.
The evening song: all sleep but one
The hall after the feast: men lying down on the benches in their cloaks with their helmets set above their heads; one man propped on his elbow, awake, his mail and his sword laid aside.
The king gives the hall into his keeping and goes to bed. He takes off his mail and hands his sword away. His men lie down sure they will never see home. All of them sleep but one.
The evening song: the grip
The hall door torn inward off its hinges; a huge manlike thing bent over the benches, its wrist caught in the grip of a man half its size; benches overturned.

Grendel comes off the moor, tears the door from its hinges, and eats a man where he lies. Then he reaches for the next, and a hand closes on his. He has never felt a grip like it. He wants only to get away.
The evening song: the arm
The monster wrenching away through the broken door into the dark, one shoulder a wound; the man left standing with a whole arm and clawed hand in his grip.
The men hack at it and no blade will bite. It does not matter. The shoulder tears, and Grendel goes home to the fen to die, and leaves his arm behind him.
The evening song: morning at Heorot
A misty morning: riders racing their horses along a track that leads back from a blood-dark pool; one rider with his head thrown back, singing.

In the morning they follow the tracks to a pool that boils with blood. Riding back they race their horses, and a king's man makes a new song on the spot, and joins to it an old one, about a man who killed a dragon.
The evening song: Hrothgar's thanks
The steps of the hall in daylight: the old king looking up at the great clawed arm hung under the gable, his hand on the young man's shoulder.
The king stands on the step, looks up at the arm hung under the roof, and thanks God. From this day, he says, he will hold the stranger as a son. And Unferth, I am glad to say, is quiet.
The evening song: the gifts
Eight horses led across the floor of the hall, one with a gold-worked saddle; the young man holding a gold banner and a helmet.
The hall is made fit again, and the king gives gifts: a gold banner, a helmet, a mail-coat, a great sword, and eight horses, one of them under the king's own saddle.
The men listen to the gifts as to a list of prices. One or two glance at the stern, where the purse is.
The evening song: the fight at Finn's fort
Evening at sea. Tonight's part of the song is about a Frisian king and the Danes who died in his hall. The steersman has heard where it is going.
A harper singing in the hall; above him, as the thing he sings: a night fight in a doorway, and a great pyre on which a woman lays a young man beside an older one.

Every man who crossed the sea with him has a gift, and gold is paid for the one who was eaten. Then the king's singer takes the harp, and sings how the Dane Hnaef fell in Finn's hall in Frisia, and how they burned the dead.
Finn was our king. I know where this goes; I have heard the English tell it. The guests are always the heroes, and the host is the one who is killed in his own hall.
Let him tell it as the English tell it
Let him tell it, and have the steersman say afterwards how Frisians tell it

He tells it as the English tell it: the Danes hold the door, and the queen burns her son and her brother on one fire. The steersman hears all of it with his face shut, and takes the dawn watch without being asked.

The lookout tells it. Then the steersman says his part, slowly: that nobody alive knows who struck first in that hall; that the song itself says Finn swore peace and kept the Danes through the winter; and that it was not Finn who broke it. The lookout says the song does not deny it. They leave it there, level.
The evening song: Finn's hall
A winter hall on a frozen shore with ships locked in the ice; inside, a grim man sitting with a naked sword that other hands have laid across his knees.

The Danes who are left winter with Finn under oath, because ice has locked the sea. In spring somebody lays a sword in their leader's lap. They kill Finn in his hall and carry his queen home, and the goods of the hall with her.
So. Guests through a whole winter, at his fire, and they killed him when the ice went out. I only say what the song says.
The evening song: the neck-ring
The queen holding out a great gold neck-ring to the young man; small and pale behind it, a dead king on a low coast with the same ring at his throat and Frankish spears standing over him.

The queen gives him a neck-ring, the best since the necklace of the Brosings. And the song stops to say where it ended: on his king Hygelac, who wore it raiding in Frisia, and the Franks had it off his body.
A king out of the north, killed raiding by the Rhine mouth. Then I have seen him. That is the thigh they show on the island.
Where the Rhine meets the sea they show a dead king's bones on an island: a man too big for any horse. I never knew he had a name, or a song.
The evening song: Grendel's mother
The sleeping hall again; a gaunt woman-shape snatching a grey-haired man up off the bench, the severed arm under her other arm; swords coming down off the walls too late.
They sleep sound, thinking it is over. It is not. Grendel had a mother, and she comes that night for the price of her son. She takes the king's dearest friend, and the arm.
The evening song: the mere
A black pool under frost-white trees that overhang a cliff, a flame burning on the water; a stag at the brink turned to face the hounds rather than go in.
The king tells where they live: a pool under frosted trees, where fire burns on the water at night. A stag run down by hounds, he says, will turn and die on the bank sooner than go in.
The evening song: the road to the mere
A man's head set on the cliff above the pool; horsemen reined in below it; one man handing a long sword hilt first to the young man, who is arming.
He says it is better for a man to avenge his friend than to mourn much. They ride to the pool and find the friend's head on the cliff. And Unferth lends him his own sword, which is a kind of sorry.
The evening song: under the water
Deep water: the hero dragged by the she-monster into a dry cave hall lit by a fire, his sword glancing off her and leaving no mark.
He says what is to be done with his gifts if he does not come back, and jumps. It is most of a day before he sees the bottom. She drags him into her hall, and the borrowed sword will not bite.
The evening song: the giants' sword
The cave hall: the hero swinging a sword too large for a man, taken down from the wall; above, small, men on the bank turning away from blood-stained water while a few stay sitting.

On the wall hangs a sword made by giants, too big for another man to carry. He kills her with it, and takes off Grendel's head. Up above, the Danes see blood come to the surface, and at the ninth hour they go home. His own men sit on, and stare at the water.
The evening song: the hilt
The old king holding a gold sword-hilt with no blade to the firelight and reading its runes; on the floor a monstrous head, carried in on a spear by four men.

The blade melted like ice in that blood, down to the hilt. He brings the hilt and the head to the king. The king looks at the gold hilt a long time: the old war of the giants is cut on it, and in runes the name of the man it was made for.
The evening song: Hrothgar's counsel
The old king and the young man alone at the high seat late at night, the king's finger raised; the hall emptying behind them, a raven on the roof beam waiting for morning.

Then the old king gives him counsel. A man is lucky, and grows proud, and begins to hoard, and forgets that it ends. Do not be that man, he says. I ruled fifty years and thought I had no enemy under the sky.
The evening song: the parting
The shore road at dawn: the white-haired king embracing the young man, tears on his face; the Geats waiting with the gift horses, and the ship's mast beyond.
They take their leave. He promises a thousand spears if the Danes should ever need them. The old king kisses him and weeps, because he is old enough to know that they will not meet again.
The evening song: the voyage home
The ship under full sail with a white wave at her bow and the gift horses aboard; on the strand behind, the boat-guard holding up a sword bound with gold.

They sail home on a fair wind; he gives the man who guarded the boat a sword bound with gold. Then the song turns to two queens: a young wise one, and one who had men killed for looking at her, until she was married to Offa of Angeln and mended.
That Offa is our king Offa's forefather, twelve fathers back, or so the Mercians reckon it. I notice the song is polite about him.
The evening song: Beowulf and Hygelac
A smaller hall by the sea: a young king and the returned hero seated face to face, a queen going down the bench with the mead cup.
His own king greets him and asks how it went, having begged him not to go. So he tells it over. And he says the king of the Danes means to marry his daughter to an old enemy's son, to mend a feud.
The evening song: the feud that will not sleep
A wedding feast: an old spearman leaning to a young man's ear and pointing across the hall at a Dane who wears a fine sword.
It will not mend, he says. Some old spearman at the wedding ale will see a Dane wearing a dead man's sword, and say to the dead man's son: do you know that blade? And it begins again.
The evening song: gifts both ways
Above: the hero leading four gift horses to his king. Below: the same man fifty years on, white-bearded on a high seat; in one corner, a dragon's eye opening in the dark.

He gives his king everything the Danes gave him, horses and all, and is given a hall and land in return. Then the song takes one breath and fifty years are gone. He is king, and old, and a dragon has woken.
The evening song: the cup
Inside a stone barrow: a ragged man creeping past the coils of a sleeping dragon with a gold cup in both hands, treasure heaped all round.

A runaway crept into a barrow and stole a cup to buy his master's pardon. The gold was laid there long before by the last man of a people, who said: hold now, earth, what men could not. The dragon found it open, and lay on it three hundred winters.
The men are very quiet for the part about the last man. Every one of them has seen a mound on a headland and wondered what was in it.
The evening song: the burning
Night: a dragon in the air pouring fire on a burning hall and its farms; in the foreground an old king watching, and behind him a smith hammering a shield all of iron.

The dragon burns the farms by night, and the king's own hall. He orders an iron shield, since wood is no use against fire. And he remembers the day his lord Hygelac fell in Frisia, and he alone swam home, with thirty men's war-gear on his arm.
Thirty men's war-gear, swimming. From our coast. Well. We would tell that day differently, I expect; but nobody has made us a song for it.
The evening song: twelve men and a guide
A headland above the sea: an old king seated on the rock, speaking; eleven armed men standing round him; a frightened thirteenth man pointing toward a stone arch in the cliff.

He goes with eleven men, and the thief for a guide, a thirteenth, who does not want to be there. On the headland he sits down and tells over his youth: how one of the old king's sons killed another with an arrow by mischance, and the old king died of a grief he could not avenge.
The evening song: the last boast
A stone arch in the cliff with a stream running hot out of it; the old king alone behind an iron shield in a blast of flame; small behind him, men running for a wood.

He tells how he crushed the Franks' champion in his bare grip. He makes his last boast, and goes down alone under the stone arch. The fire comes. His sword bites less than he needed. And the chosen men behind him run for the wood.
The evening song: Wiglaf
A young warrior plunging through smoke, a wooden shield burning on his arm, to stand beside the old king, whose sword has just snapped at the hilt.

All but one. A young kinsman, Wiglaf, who has never yet fought. He reminds the rest what they promised over the mead, and goes in through the smoke. His shield burns to the boss. The old king's sword breaks.
We have a saying at home. It is a thegn's choice to stand fast beside his lord. One in eleven chose it. That is about the number.
The evening song: the end of the fight
The dragon's jaws closed on the old king's neck; the young man driving his sword in low; the king's free hand drawing a knife.

The dragon has him by the neck. The young man strikes it low, and the old one draws his knife and cuts it through the middle. So they killed it between them. But the bite burns and swells. He asks to see the gold he has paid for.
The evening song: Beowulf's barrow
The old king propped against the barrow wall, dying, with gold heaped at his knees; he gives his neck-ring and his helmet to the young man, and points out to a headland over the sea.

The young man carries out as much gold as his arms will hold. The king thanks God that he could win it for his people, and asks for a mound on the Whale's Ness, built high, so that men who drive their ships from far over the dark water will call it Beowulf's barrow. Then he dies.
The steersman, who steers by such mounds, nods at that.
The evening song: the ten who ran
Ten men with unmarked shields coming shamefaced out of a wood; the young warrior kneeling by the dead king with water in his cupped hands, looking up at them.

The ten come out of the wood, ashamed, carrying their shields. The young man is still throwing water on the king's face. He tells them what their names will be worth from this day, and their kin's, and that death would have been better.
The evening song: the messenger
A rider on the cliff edge speaking down to a camp of seated warriors, every face lifted to him; one of his arms pointing south across the sea.

A rider carries the news to the people. He says: now the Franks and the Frisians will hear that our king is dead, and they have not forgotten Hygelac's raid. And the Swedes have a longer memory still.
He is right that we had not forgotten. People who are raided do not. It is the raiders who are surprised.
The evening song: Ravenswood
A dark wood full of ravens, a white-haired king of the Swedes at bay among shields; in the foreground a raven and an eagle on a dead man.

He tells the old war with the Swedes, and the fight at Ravenswood. Then he says: no harp will wake the warriors now; the raven will tell the eagle how he fared at the meal. They go and look. The dragon lies fifty feet long.
The evening song: the hoard carried out
Torchlight: seven men carrying treasure out of the mouth of the barrow; others levering the dragon's long body over the cliff into the sea.

Seven men carry the hoard out by torchlight. They push the dragon over the cliff and let the sea have it. The gold goes on a wagon with the king. There was a curse on it, the song says, and it did nobody any good.
The evening song: the burning of Beowulf
Evening at sea. The lookout says tonight's part is the last.
A great pyre hung with helmets and shields burning on a headland, a woman with her hair unbound lamenting; beside it a new mound with twelve riders circling it; ships far out on the sea.

They build the pyre and hang it with helmets and shields, and a woman of the Geats sings what is coming to them now. Ten days they are building the mound. All the gold goes into it. Twelve riders go round it and say he was the mildest of kings, the kindest to his people, and the keenest for a good name.
Nobody speaks. The water runs along the strakes. After a time the mate says that was a long way to row for one grave, and that he is glad he came.
The singer's pay
The lookout has given you a whole song, forty-three evenings of it. The mate thinks that is worth something.
A calm evening at sea: the lookout sitting in the bow with his hands empty and open on his knees, the song finished; the mate half turned toward the merchant with one finger raised, about to speak.
Forty-three evenings. In a hall, a man who can do that is given a ring off the lord's own arm. He will not ask. So I ask.
It is not mine. I had it from an old brother who learned it before he took his vows. I only carried it, as we carry wine.
Weigh him out the worth of an arm-ring (12 d)
A new cloak cut from the cargo's cloth
Thank him before the others, and ask him to begin it again for the next hand who has not heard it

Twelve pennies' weight, counted out before the crew. He goes red and tries to give it back, and the mate closes his hand over it for him. A singer has been paid in this boat. The men sit a little straighter, as if she were a hall.
A cloak's length is cut from the bolt, good Frisian weave: the first whole new thing he has owned since the cloister. He sleeps warm in it that night. The mate remarks that it is long enough.
You say it before them all, and ask him to begin again when there is a new man to hear it. He says he will. He is pleased and trying not to be, as his masters taught him.
